editionLabel: Pegasus Spiele German rules, English summary

editionLabel: Pegasus Spiele German Sagrada rules, four-page sheet, English summary
location: Spielvorbereitung: Allgemeine Vorbereitung, E; Spielablauf; Solovariante
firstPlayerRule: Whoever most recently visited Barcelona goes first.
clarifications: The first player takes the dice bag and begins the first pass. The second pass runs in reverse order, so the last player takes two turns in succession.

evidenceNotes: The Barcelona criterion was read on the rendered German sheet. A starting instruction from a different language or edition was not substituted.

editionLabel: Pegasus Spiele German rules, takenoko-anleitung.pdf, English summary
firstPlayerRule: The player whose head is highest above the ground goes first.
clarifications: Turns continue clockwise. Every player skips the weather roll on their own first turn.
uncertainty: The source does not specify posture or a method of measuring head height.
evidenceNotes: The unusual head-above-ground wording is explicit; it has not been silently changed to body height.

editionLabel: Pegasus Spiele German rules, English summary
firstPlayerRule: Choose the starter with a quantum random generator, or another method the group considers sufficiently random if one is unavailable.
officialTieBreak: Without a quantum random generator, the rules explicitly allow any other method with a degree of randomness the group accepts.
clarifications: The selected person takes the first turn, followed clockwise. Solo play has a separate sequence for its single player.
evidenceNotes: The alternative is an official instruction, not a house fallback. No claim is made that this website uses a quantum generator. Campaign cards and hidden content were not opened.

editionLabel: Pegasus Spiele German base rules, English summary
firstPlayerRule: The most easily contented player goes first.
clarifications: The starter draws five cards. The remaining players, in clockwise order, draw six, seven and eight cards as applicable.
uncertainty: The German criterion is genügsamste: most content with little or least demanding. The source supplies no objective test.
evidenceNotes: The criterion is translated from this German file rather than importing the wording of an English edition. Printed page 5 is PDF page 6.
interpretation: Here, the German word genügsamste means being content with little. The rule gives no objective test.
